analysis.one_liner: Bans forced arbitration and class-action waivers in employment, consumer, antitrust, and civil rights disputes.
analysis.headline: The bill has sat in the House Judiciary Committee since September 2025 with no hearing, no vote, and 70 Democratic cosponsors and no Republican ones.
analysis.plain_summary: Most people sign contracts—when hired, when opening a bank account, when buying a phone—surrendering their right to sue and to join class actions, and instead must use private arbitration chosen by the company. The bill would make those pre-dispute arbitration agreements unenforceable for employment, consumer, antitrust, and civil rights disputes. People could still choose arbitration after a dispute actually arises, and union contracts with arbitration would stay intact.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers, consumers, and small businesses who are currently bound by forced arbitration clauses and class-action waivers. They would regain the right to take disputes to a public court, join class actions, and have a judge—not the company—decide whether the rule applies. This matters most in cases like wage theft, discrimination, and defective products, where individual claims are too small to bring alone and a class action is the only realistic remedy.

how_it_helps.text: The bill voids pre-dispute arbitration agreements and pre-dispute class-action waivers for employment, consumer, antitrust, and civil rights disputes, restoring access to court [S2].
A court, not an arbitrator, decides whether the law applies, even if the contract tries to delegate that decision to an arbitrator [S2].
Arbitration remains allowed if both sides choose it voluntarily after a dispute actually arises [S2].
Arbitration in union collective bargaining agreements is preserved, except workers keep the right to go to court to enforce constitutional and statutory rights [S2].
The definitions cover independent contractors as well as employees, closing a common workaround for gig workers [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Companies that use forced arbitration clauses—large employers, banks, telecoms, credit card issuers, and app-based platforms—would lose a system that limits their legal exposure, keeps disputes confidential, and blocks class actions. They would face more court litigation, including class actions, and higher legal costs. Some of those costs could be passed to consumers through prices; small businesses using standard contracts would also see changes.

drawbacks.text: Opponents argue arbitration can be faster and cheaper for an individual worker than court, and that some workers knowingly prefer it; the bill keeps voluntary arbitration only after a dispute arises, removing the option people might bargain for up front [S2].

Opening more disputes to court and to class actions would raise litigation costs for companies, including small businesses relying on standard contracts; companies may pass some of these costs on through prices, and class actions can produce small individual payouts while lawyers take large fees [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit—regaining the right to sue and join class actions—is large for the tens of millions of people bound by these clauses, because forced arbitration is private, decided by a company-chosen arbitrator, typically with no appeal and no group remedy for small individual harms. The cost is real but diffuse: more litigation expense for companies and possible price effects. On balance the bill trades a modest, spread-out cost for a significant, concentrated-in-the-public benefit.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the House Judiciary Committee, which has not taken it up, so it sits without a hearing or a vote while Congress remains in session.

narrative.text: Rep. Hank Johnson introduced the FAIR Act on September 15, 2025, and it was referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary [S4].
The bill's sole action since referral is the referral itself; there is no hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor action in the record [S4].
It has 70 cosponsors, all Democrats; no Republican cosponsor has joined [S3].

The bill would render pre-dispute arbitration agreements and class-action waivers unenforceable in employment, consumer, antitrust, and civil rights disputes, while preserving voluntary post-dispute arbitration and union collective bargaining agreements [S2].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, companies with forced arbitration clauses are better off: the status quo they built remains untouched, with no hearing or vote in the committee that controls the bill's fate.

for.name: Rep. Hank Johnson
for.what_they_did: Introduced the FAIR Act and referred it to the House Judiciary Committee.

for.name: 70 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, making it a broadly supported House Democratic measure with no Republican cosponsors.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: Has not scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill since its September 2025 referral, keeping it from any vote.

sides.party_line_note: All 70 cosponsors are Democrats and there are no Republican cosponsors; the House is controlled by Republicans, whose committee chair has taken no action on the bill [S3][S4].

industries.note: Forced arbitration clauses and class-action waivers shield these companies from court, from group lawsuits, and from public scrutiny of wage, discrimination, and misconduct claims. The bill would remove that shield for work-related disputes [S2].

industries.industry: Consumer-facing corporations (banks, credit card issuers, telecoms, retailers)
industries.note: These firms use arbitration clauses and class-action waivers in standard consumer contracts, which limits collective legal action over fees, fraud, and defective products. The bill would let consumers take those disputes to court or a class action [S2].
Mandated arbitration is a paid service; invalidating pre-dispute clauses shrinks the pipeline of forced cases, though voluntary post-dispute arbitration survives [S2].

Lawyers who bring employment, consumer, antitrust, and civil rights class actions would see a much larger universe of viable cases, which is also the mechanism through which workers and consumers recover.

analysis.trajectory: With a Republican-controlled House, no Republican cosponsors, and no hearing or markup scheduled, the bill is very unlikely to advance this Congress. Versions of this bill have repeatedly stalled at this stage in past sessions; the realistic path is that it stays in committee and is reintroduced in a future Congress.
